The story achieves an exceptional balance between interiority and exteriority, demonstrating strong emotional flexibility. 

In the first half, the narrator's complex interior life—his love, envy, and feelings of inadequacy toward Q—is grounded in vivid exterior details (the goose lamp, the list in the geology notebook, the incident with the campus officer). 

In the second half, the hotel pool scene weaves the two seamlessly together. The exterior plot drives the momentum through the awkward, overheard dialogue between Q and Dana and physical descriptions of the setting (the blue goggles, Q's hands flat on the table, his tie swinging). Simultaneously, the narrator's interiority interprets the emotional weight of the moment ("the way you know a glass will fall a half second before it does"). Finally, the story showcases great emotional flexibility when the narrator gets the "flaw" he waited ten years to see, only for his long-held resentment to unexpectedly shift into a "terrible tenderness" and empathy.
